lineages.name: Chuck Berry
lineages.why: Made the guitar riff the song's main melodic element and grafted country guitar licks onto an R&B chassis, with electronic effects mimicking bottleneck players. Wrote humorous, specific lyrics about teen dances, cars and school on records from Maybellene to Johnny B. Goode.

lineages.name: Jimmy Page (Led Zeppelin)
lineages.why: Produced When the Levee Breaks with Bonham's kit miked by two M160s over the Headley Grange stairwell through heavily driven Helios compressors, parts recorded fast and slowed down, and reverse echo. He and John Paul Jones replaced the twelve-bar with a one-chord modal drone.

lineages.name: Butch Vig
lineages.why: Produced Nevermind with overdubs and double-tracked vocals and guitars, persuading Cobain by pointing out that John Lennon double-tracked. The polish (with Andy Wallace's mix) set the loud-quiet alternative rock template.

lineages.name: Steve Albini
lineages.why: Called himself a recording engineer, not a producer, and recorded bands live together with few overdubs, minimal compression and natural room reverb, to analogue tape. Usually recorded and mixed an album in about a week (Surfer Rosa, In Utero).

name: Rock

notes.text: The standard beat: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, constant eighth notes on the hi-hat; common variants add the kick on the and-of-3 or put it on every quarter.
IV is the commonest chord after I (0.226 of all chords), then V (0.163), bVII (0.081) and VI (0.072). IV precedes the tonic more often than V does, and V-I mostly occurs inside IV-V-I.

Root motion is symmetric: ascending and descending fourths are equally common, and frequency falls with distance on the circle of fifths. bVII, bIII and bVI tend to occur together (mixolydian/aeolian borrowing).
Modal and one-chord writing is normal: When the Levee Breaks drops the twelve-bar form for a one-chord drone, and melodies draw on dorian and mixolydian as much as major and minor.
Distorted guitar plays power chords (root and fifth, no third) because the 3:2 ratio stays coherent under distortion where full triads turn to mush.

Loud-quiet contrast is a structural tool: quiet verses with chorused clean guitar, then big distorted choruses (the Smells Like Teen Spirit template). Rhythm guitars are usually double-tracked; Vig got Cobain to double-track guitar and vocals.
Verse-refrain form from blues and folk, in 4-, 8- and 12-bar sections: Smells Like Teen Spirit has an 8-bar verse, 8-bar pre-chorus, 12-bar chorus and a post-chorus.

Typical moves: drums on their own bus with about 2:1 and a couple of dB of compression, a heavily squashed parallel bus under drums, bass and vocals, distorted guitars band-limited (high-pass near 250 Hz, low-pass near 3.7 kHz), gentle 2:1 master bus with about 2 dB on loud sections.

Released rock masters: median -9.2 LUFS (middle half -11.0 to -7.8) in the largest survey; a smaller sample puts rock at -12.1 with the widest loudness range of any genre (10.7 LU). Crest factor fell sharply between 1985 and 2010 in the loudness war.
The drum sound is often the room: Bonham's Levee drums were two M160s hung over a stairwell at Headley Grange through aggressively set Helios compressors so the kit 'breathes'.
From Chuck Berry on, rock lyrics carry humorous, concrete detail of teen life: dances, cars, school, consumer goods and the music itself.
The guitar riff is a primary melodic element alongside the vocal; Berry made the riff the lead line of the song.

pitfalls.text: Writing rock changes like classical or pop cadences, always V-I. In rock IV and bVII precede the tonic as often as V; use IV-I, bVII-IV-I and modal vamps.
Full major/minor triads on distorted guitar. They go muddy; use root-fifth power chords and let bass and vocal supply the third.
Same density everywhere. Rock choruses lift through contrast: thin the verse (clean guitar, fewer layers) so the distorted chorus lands.

progressions.text: IV-V-I is the commonest trigram ending on the tonic (352 instances); where V precedes the tonic, IV almost always precedes V.
bVII is the third most frequent chord before the tonic and a common predecessor of IV; the double-plagal move is rock's own cadence.
Smells Like Teen Spirit's four power chords (F5-Bb5-Ab5-Db5) under verse, pre-chorus and chorus alike.
The 'backwards' rock cadence, second only to IV-V-I among trigrams ending on the tonic (292 instances).

summary: Band music centred on the amplified electric guitar over bass and drums, in 4/4 with a snare backbeat on 2 and 4 and a verse-refrain form inherited from blues and folk. Its harmony is not common-practice: IV is used more than V, bVII is the fourth commonest chord, and roots move by fourths up and down equally.
